1.x: “And it came to pass, that when Jesus had finished these sayings…”: This is a structural formula Matthew uses fives times to signal the end of a major teaching discourse (see also Mt 17:28; 11:1; 13:53, and 26:1). It bridges the transition from Christ’s verbal instruction back to his public ministry and movement. “..he departed from Galilee..”: For most of his earthly ministry, Galilee had been Jesus’ home base. It was a region filled with fertile hills, towns, and a diverse population. By leaving Galilee, Jesus is closing the door on that phrase of his ministry. Luke 9:51 parallel notes that he “steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem.” “...and came into the coasts of Judaea beyond Jordan”: The word “coats” (horion in Greek) simply means borders, regions, or territories. To avoid traveling straight through hostile Samaria, Jesus takes the standard Jewish travel route of the day. He crosses to the eastern side of the Jordan River into a region known as Perea (which literally means “beyond” or “the other side”). Perea was politically grouped with Galilee under the rule of Herod Antipas, but topographically and socially, it bordered Judea to the east.

2.x: Even though Jesus has changed regions and crossed the river, his fame precedes him. The local populations recognize him, and massive crowds gather around him along the travel route. “..and he healed them there”: This brief summary statement highlights Christ’s unrelenting compassion. Despite the looming weight of the crucifixion awaiting him in Jerusalem, and despite the fact that he is actively traveling, he does not withdraw from human need. By explicitly noting that he healed them “there” (in Perea/beyond the Jordan), Matthew underscores that Christ’s power, authority, and saving mercy are not confined to the religious centers or the home territories of Galilee (remember Jews had to travel to the temple in Jerusalem for their sacrifices). Wherever the multitudes gather to meet him IN FAITH, his healing power is fully present.

3.x: “..tempting him..”: The Pharisees are not seeking truth; they are setting a theological trap. In first-century Judaism, two major rabbinic schools debated Deut 24:1 (which allowed divorce if a husband found some “uncleanness” in his wife). The strict School of Shammai taught that divorce was only permissible for marital unfaithfulness. The lenient School of Hillel taught that a man could divorce his wife “for every cause,” including burning his dinner or simply finding a more attractive woman. This was a political trap. Jesus is in Perea, the territory of Herod Antipas. Herod had famously arrested and executed John the Baptist for speaking out against Herod’s unlawful divorce and remarriage to Herodias. The Pharisees hope Jesus will say something that either alienates the crowds or alerts Herod’s authorities.

4.x: “Have ye not read…”: Jesus immediately exposes their shallow understanding of scripture. Instead of refereeing a debate between human traditions (Shammai vs Hillel), he appeals directly to the written Word of God (Gen 1:27). “.. at the beginning..”: Jesus establishes that the ultimate standard for marriage is found in God’s original creation design, prior to the introduction of human sin, cultural decay, or the concessions of the Mosaic civil code. “..made them male and female..”: Jesus underscores that God intentionally created human beings with a purposeful, biological, and binary distinction. The differences between man and woman are not arbitrary; they are hardcoded into creation by the Architect of humanity.

5.x: “And said..”: Jesus quotes Genesis 2:24. He attributes the words of Genesis directly to God Himself, framing it as an absolute, timeless divine decree. “For this cause..”: Because God created them male and female, human sexuality has a specific trajectory. “..shall a man leave.. And shall cleave to his wife..”: Jesus defines the relational structure of marriage. It requires a biological male (a man) and a biological female (his wife) separating from their families of origin to form a new, lifelong covenantal unit. “..and they twain shall be one flesh?”: The archain word “twain” means two. Two distinct, biologically complementary genders come together to form an organic, holistic unity. This “one(mia: feminine singular one) flesh(a single feminine word)” union encompasses spiritual, emotional, and physical/procreative binding that is physically impossible apart from gender complementarity.

6.x: “..no more twain, but one flesh”: Marriage fundamentally alters the metaphysical reality of the couple. In God’s eyes, they are no longer viewed as two independent items, but as a singular entity. “What therefore God hath joined together…”: Marriage is not merely a human social contract, a romantic feeling, or a civil arrangement. It is a divine action. God is the one who binds the male and female together when they enter this covenant. “..let not man put asunder”: Because God did the joining, no human court, human tradition, or human desire has the moral authority to dissolve or alter what God has established.

Jesus’ statement contradicts homosexual marriage. Those who argue for homosexual marriage often note that Jesus never explicitly uses the word “homosexuality” in the gospels. However, Jesus does not need to explicitly forbid every counterfeit form of marriage because HE EXPLICITLY DEFINES WHAT MARRIAGE ACTUALLY IS: (1) Jesus states that marriage exists explicitly because God “made them male and female” (v.4). In Christ’s theology, gender is not a social construct or a fluid spectrum; it is a fixed, binary reality designed by God. The entire framework of marriage relies on the existence of these two different genders coming together. A same-sex union lacks the ontological “male-and-female” baseline that Jesus states is foundational to the institution. (2) In v.5, Jesus explicitly identifies the two components that make up the “twain”: a man (singular male) and his wife(singular female). Christ’s math for marriage is strictly 1 male + 1 female = 1 flesh. Any configuration that alters these specific components, whether it is polygamist (1 man + multiple women) or homosexual (1 man + 1 man) violates the formula Jesus laid down. (3) The “one flesh” union (v.5-6) is both a spiritual covenant and a physical, biological reality. Anatomically and procreatively, the male and female bodies are designed to fit together to generate new human life, completing the creation mandate. Same-sex unions cannot achieve this biological “one flesh” integration as designed by the Creator at the beginning.

Jesus demonstrates exactly how God expects human beings to read, interpret, and apply holy scripture: (1) Read for original intent, not loopholes: The Pharisees read scripture to find legalistic escape clauses (“Is it lawful..for every cause?”). They wanted to know how far they could push the boundaries of the Law without technically sinning. Jesus expects us to read scripture to find God’s heart and original design, seeking absolute obedience rather than technical exemptions. (2) The authority from the beginning: Jesus establishes that newer cultural developments, human traditions, or even temporary civil concessions (like Moses allowing divorce letters due to the “hardness of hearts” in v.8) must always be corrected by the unchanging standard of God’s initial creation. Truth does not evolve with cultural consensus. (3) Scripture is globally harmonious: Jesus flawlessly links Genesis 1:27 (the creation of gender) with Genesis 2:24(the institution of marriage). He expects us to read the Bible synthetically, understanding that different passages of scripture DO NOT CONTRADICT EACH OTHER, but rather build upon one another to form a cohesive moral framework. (4) God speaks directly through the text: In v.5, Jesus quotes Genesis 2:24 (which was written by the narrator of Genesis) and says: “And [God] said..” Jesus reads scripture with the absolute conviction that the words of the text are the literal, living voice of God the Father (the divine Spirit). To read scripture correctly is to listen to the active decrees of the Creator.

7.x: “They say unto him, Why did Moses then command..”: The Pharisees think they have found an unanswerable contradiction. They frame Deut 24:1 (“When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house.”,KJV) as a commandment to divorce. In their minds, if God’s original plan was lifelong unity, then Moses was acting against God by ordering men to issue divorce certificates. They are attempting to pit scripture against scripture, and Moses against Jesus. “..to give a writing of divorcement…”: The “writing of divorcement” (the Hebrew “get”) was a formal legal document. In the ancient world, a discarded woman was highly vulnerable, often facing destitution or starvation. The document was actually a legal protection for the woman; it officially proved she was no longer bound to her husband, clearing her of any charges of adultery and legally permitting her to remarry to secure a livelihood. The Pharisees, however, had twisted this protective legal mechanism into an easy exit pass for men.

8.x: “He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts…”: Jesus completely alters their premise. Moses did not command or institute divorce; he tolerated it as a civil concession. The root cause was human rebellion and spiritual corruption: the “hardness of your hearts.” God knew that without this legal boundary, hard-hearted men would simply abandon, abuse, or falsely accuse their wives to rid themselves of them. The law was given to manage the fallout of human sin, not to express God’s moral ideal. “..suffered you to put away your wives…”: Jesus makes a profound linguistic correction. The Pharisees used the word “command” (v.7), but Jesus replaces it with “suffered” (permitted/tolerated). There is a vast difference between what God commands in holiness and what God permits in His patience due to human failure. “..but from the beginning it was not so”: Jesus completely strips the Pharisees of their legal loophole by re-establishing the absolute standard. He bypasses Deut and returns to Genesis. Civil laws may shift to handle the broken realities of a fallen world, but God’s original moral design for humanity remains completely unchanged. Cultural norms, legal provisions, and human weakness can never alter the primordial definition of marriage.

9.x: “And I say unto you..”: Jesus speaks with his own divine authority (“I say”), superseding the rabbinic traditions and clarifying the true spiritual weight of the Mosaic law. “...except it be for fornication..”: This is the famous “exception clause.” The Greek word used in “porneia,” a broad term for sexual immorality, including adultery, incest, or pre-marital sex. Sexual immorality fundamentally violates and shatters the “one flesh” covenant established by God. It is not a command to divorce, but a tragic permission because the covenant has already been broken by the offending partner. “..and shall marry another, committeth adultery..”: If a man divorces his wife without the ground of “porneia” and remarries, God does not recognize the divorce. In the eyes of heaven, the original marriage bond remains active; therefore, entering a new physical union constitutes adultery. “..and whose marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery”: Similarly, marrying a woman who was divorced on unbiblical grounds involves entering an illegitimate union, because her original covenantal bond was never divinely dissolved.

10.x: “His disciples say unto him..”: The disciples are stunned by the strictness of Jesus’ teaching. Growing up in a culture heavily influenced by the lenient School of Hillel (which allowed easy divorce), they realize the immense, lifelong weight of the marriage vow. “..it is not good to mary”: Their response is pragmatic, bordering on cynical. They reason that if a man is permanently locked into a marriage with no escape hatch (even if the marriage becomes deeply difficult or unhappy) it is safer and better to never enter the covenant in the first place.

11.x: “But he said unto them, All men cannot receive this saying…”: Jesus does not scold them for their shock, but he corrects their logic. Remaining unmarried and celibate is not an easy lifestyle choice that anyone can simply opt into out of fear or convenience. “...save they to whom it is given”: Lifelong celibacy requires a specific sovereign enablement from God. It is a supernatural gift (charisma), not merely an act of human willpower. Without this divine enablement, forcing oneself into isolation can lead to intense temptation.

12.x: Jesus breaks down the three distinct categories of “eunuchs,” a term historically used for men who were castrated, but contextually used here by Jesus to describe anyone who abstains from marriage and sexual relations: (1) “..born so from their mother’s womb”: These are individuals born with congenital birth defects, physical developments, or a natural lack of sexual disposition that prevents them from marrying or procreating. (2) “..made eunuchs of men”: This refers to the brutal ancient practice where kings and rulers castrated servants or slaves to secure them as safe guardians over royal harems(secluded quarters in a royal palace where a king’s wives, concubines, and female relatives lived). This was an externally forced physical condition. (3) “..which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake”: This is the spiritual core of the verse. Jesus is not advocating for physical self-mutilation (which was strictly forbidden under Mosaic law: “He that is wounded in the stones, or hath his privy member cut off, shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord.” Deut 23:1, KJV). Instead, he is speaking metaphorically of those who voluntarily choose lifelong celibacy to devote their undivided time, energy, and focus to serving God’s kingdom without the earthly responsibilities of a spouse and children (a theme Paul expands on in 1 Cor 7). “He that is able to receive it, let him receive it”: Jesus closes by reinforcing that this path is a specialized calling. It is not a universal requirement for all believers, nor is it a morally superior status; it is a unique station of grace for those equipped by God to handle it.

While the Roman Catholic Church uses Mt 19:12 to defend its mandate of clerical celibacy, a strict biblical and historical analysis reveals that Christ’s words do not support the Roman Catholic system. The text directly contradicts the Catholic implementation of this practice in three fundamental ways: (1) The most glaring contradiction lies in the contrast between voluntary choice and compulsory law. Jesus says: “He that is able to receive it, let him receive it” (v.12). Jesus leaves this path entirely optional, framing it as a choice made by an individual who recognizes they have been given the specific spiritual gift to handle it (v.11). Rome says: Canon 277 of the Roman Catholic Code of Canon Law strictly mandates celibacy for all Latin-rite priests. By legally binding celibacy to the office of the priesthood, the Roman Catholic Church transforms what Jesus defined as a sovereignly distributed spiritual gift into an institutional requirement for employment. If an individual has a genuine calling to preach the gospel but does not possess the specific spiritual gift of celibacy, Rome forbids them from ministry. This runs completely counter to Christ’s teaching that “all men cannot receive this saying” (v.11). (2) Scripture explicitly allows ministers to marry. If Mt 19 was meant to establish a standard where gospel ministers must remain unmarried, the apostles themselves would have been in violation of Christ’s teaching. The NT consistently demonstrates that marriage and ministry are fully compatible: Peter was married. In Mt 8:14, Jesus physically heals Peter’s wife’s mother. Peter (whom Rome claims as the first Pope) was a married man throughout his entire time walking with Jesus. The apostles were married as well. Years after the resurrection, the apostle Paul defends his ministerial rights by writing: "Have we not power to lead about a sister, A WIFE, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas [Peter]?" (1 Cor 9:5, KJV). And Bishops are assumed to be married. When Paul lays down the divine qualifications for church leadership, he explicitly assumes that pastors and bishops will be married: "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife... One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection..." (1 Tim 3:2-4, KJV). (3) Far from supporting a mandatory celibacy rule for clergy, the NT issues a severe warning against any religious system that attempts to legally forbid marriage to its adherents. In 1 Tim 4:1-3, Paul writes under the direct inspiration of the Spirit: “Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils; Speaking lies in hypocrisy; having their conscience seared with a hot iron; FORBIDDING TO MARRY, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth” (KJV). By creating an ecclesiastical law that strictly forbids its massive workforce of priests, monks, and nuns from entering the holy covenant of marriage, the Roman system aligns directly with the description warnings Paul laid down regarding the departure from the apostolic faith. Jesus highly honors those who choose to remain single to advance the Kingdom of God. However, he presents it as a specialized, individual calling, not a wholesale restriction for church office. Rome’s enforcement of clerical celibacy replaces Christ’s framework of grace with a rigid human tradition.

13.x: “little children”: The Greek word used here is “paidia,” which denotes very young children, toddlers, or infants (the parallel account in Lk 18:15 explicitly uses the word “brephe,” which means “infants” or “babies”). These children were completely dependent on others to bring them to Jesus. “That he should put his hands on them, and pray”: The parents brought the infants for a blessing and intercessory prayer. They were not bringing them to be baptized, initiated into a ritual, or to perform any religious sacrament. “And the disciples rebuked them”: The disciples viewed the infants as an interruption to Jesus’ serious theological discourses. In the ancient world, children held low social status and were seen as lacking the capacity for intellectual understanding or social contribution.

14.x: “Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me”: “Suffer” in the KJV means to “allow” or “permit.” Jesus sternly corrects his disciples, removing any barrier between himself and the infants. “For of such in the kingdom of heaven”: This is the crucial theological statement. Jesus does not say the kingdom WILL belong to them if they perform a future ritual. He states that the kingdom of heaven currently, ALREADY belongs to “such” as these. It indicates that infants and young children inherently possess the status of kingdom citizens.

15.x: “And he laid his hands on them”: Jesus bestows his blessing directly upon them. He does not administer a sacrament, nor does he instruct his disciples to perform any ceremonial rite or ritual cleansing on them. He simply receives them, blesses them, and affirms their acceptance.

Many ecclesiastical traditions, most notably the Roman Catholic Church, teach that infants are born under the absolute condemnation of original sin and cannot enter heaven unless they receive the sacrament of water baptism to wash it away. According to Catholic dogma, baptism is the mechanical instrument of justification for an infant. Mt 19:13-15 completely contradicts this sacramental theology by demonstrating that infants are already secure in Christ’s kingdom without any physical ritual. First, when the infants were brought to Jesus, he had the perfect opportunity to establish infant baptism or a similar rite if it were necessary for their salvation, yet Jesus DID NOT baptize them, DID NOT command the disciples to baptize them, DID NOT perform any sacramental work. He merely prayed for them and blessed them. If a sacrament were required to save a baby from hell, Jesus would have been withholding a necessary means of grace from these children. Instead, he pronounced them citizens of the kingdom exactly as they were. Secondly, Jesus uses the present tense of: “Of such IS the kingdom of heaven.” He states that the kingdom of heaven BELONGS to these little children. An infant has no cognitive capability to understand theology, repent of personal sin, or make a confession of faith. Because they cannot understand the law or consciously choose to rebel against God, they are held under God’s grace, safe from the condemnation of sin until they reach a personal age of accountability (when they can consciously choose or reject God’s truth). If the kingdom belongs to them in their natural, un-baptized state, then an infant who dies before undergoing any religious ritual or sacrament goes directly to heaven. Their salvation is secured by Christ’s grace, independent of human ceremony. Thirdly, Jesus takes this principle a step further by using the infant AS THE BASELINE STANDARD for how adults must be saved: "Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." (Mt 18:3 KJV). An infant does not earn salvation through works, merits, or religious rituals; an infant simply exists as a helpless recipient of care. By stating that adults must become like little children to be saved, Jesus demonstrates that salvation is received entirely as a gift of grace through faith, wholly independent of sacramental rituals, institutional systems, or human works.

16.x: “Good Master”: The young man addresses Jesus as a respected rabbi (“Master” or “Teacher”), appending the honorific “Good.” However, he views Jesus merely as an exceptional human teacher, not as God manifest in the flesh. “What good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?”: The man’s theology is fundamentally based on human merit and legalism. He believes eternal life is a commodity to be earned through a specific, extraordinary act of righteousness (“what good thing shall I do”) rather than a gift received through faith.

17.x: “Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is, God”: A Trinitarian sees God-the-Father(“God”) as distinct from God-the-Son(“Jesus”). They would explain this verse like: “Jesus does not deny that He is God; rather, he challenges the young man’s casual use of the word ‘good.’ Jesus is forcing a logical dilemma: ‘If only God is truly good, and you recognize Me as good, are you prepared to acknowledge that I am God?’ “ For Oneness Christians, this is different. Oneness differentiate between the divine Spirit that is the only true God (Jn 4:24; 17:3; 1 Tim 2:5), and the visible temple and image of this invisible Spirit: the authentic human being, the man Jesus (Jn 2:19; Col 1:15; 2:9-10). Hence, this verse clearly shows the distinction between the humanity of the Son and the deity of the Father indwelling him. So when Jesus says: “there is none good but one(heis: singular masculine one), that is, God,” he is affirming the absolute oneness of God (by using the singular masculine Greek pronoun “heis”; if God was a “unity of persons”, Matthew would have used “hen”, the neuter form of one). He gives an explicit endorsement of the Jewish Shema (Deut 6:4). It establishes that God is an absolute numerical singularity (“one”). God is the sole source, definition, and standard of absolute goodness. The man Jesus lived and spoke on earth as a true human being. When the ruler approached him as merely a human rabbi, Jesus responded OUT OF HIS HUMAN CONSCIOUSNESS. As a man (not as a second divine person of the Trinity) walking in complete submission to the Father, Jesus refused to accept self-glorifying titles or human flattery. By saying “Why callest thou me good?” Jesus-as-man was re-directing all glory, praise, and credit to the divine Spirit: the Father who dwelt within him (Jn 14:10; Col 2:9; 2 Cor 5:19). But, similar to the Trinitarian explanation, Jesus is not denying that he is God in the flesh (even though Trinitarians claim he is God-the-Son, while Oneness claim he is the One God indwelling the flesh), rather Jesus is setting a trap of logic for the rich young ruler: (1) Only God is truly good; (2) You have just observed and confessed that I am good; (3) Therefore, to be consistent, you must recognize that I am God (the YHWH of the OT) manifested in the flesh. Jesus is testing whether the man will look past his outward humanity and recognize the absolute deity of the Father operating through him. “But if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments”: Jesus meets the man on his own legalistic ground. Since the man asked what work he must do to be saved, Jesus points him to the perfect standard of God’s Law. Jesus knows no human can keep the commandments perfectly (“Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in His sight” Rom 3:20 KJV). Before showing him the way to life, Jesus wanted to impress on the young man both the high standard required by God and the absolute futility of seeking salvation by his own merit: “For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all” (Jms 2:10 KJV). This should have elicited a response about the impossibility of keeping the law perfectly, like how the disciples did in v. 25: “When his disciples heard it, they were exceedingly amazed, saying, Who then can be saved?” (KJV), but instead the young man confidently, wrongly declared that he qualified for heaven under those terms (v.20).

Matthew 19:17 has a variant between the TR/MT and the CT. Bibles based on the TR (like KJV, NKJV, MEV, Reina-Valera, etc), render this verse like: "Why CALLEST THOU ME GOOD? there is none good but one, that is, God..." (KJV). While modern translations based on the CT (like ESV, NIV, NASB, LSB, NRSV, BSB), render this verse as: “Why do you ask Me about WHAT IS GOOD?.. There is only One who is good” (BSB). The CT alters Jesus’ opening question from an inquiry into his identity (“Why callest thou ME good?”) to an inquiry into the topic of discussion (“Why do you ask me about WHAT IS good?”). This is yet another reason why I trust the TR/MT more than the CT (although I appreciate what the CT contributes). The CT OVERCORRECTED by sticking to the two oldest Greek manuscripts we have. Even though they’re both from the Alexandrian family (Egypt), they still decided to give them too much authority in determining Scriptural variants. Only 0.2% of Greek manuscripts support the CT, while 97.7% support the TR/MT rendering (percentages come from “The Text-Critical English NT” by Robert Adam Boyd). Also, the Bible interprets itself: the accounts in Mark and Luke are identical to the KJV reading of Matthew, and there is no textual dispute in those gospels: (1) "Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God." (Mk 10:18 KJV); (2) "Why callest thou me good? none is good, save one, that is, God." (Lk 18:19 KJV). IF the CT is correct, it means Matthew recorded a completely different philosophical question (“Why ask me about WHAT IS good?”) than Mark and Luke, despite recording the exact same narrative context. The TR/MT reading maintains perfect harmony across all three Synotic accounts, showing that Jesus was addressing the young man’s flattery rather than deflecting a philosophical question about ethics. In the TR/MT reading, Jesus’ statement (“there is none good but one, that is, God”) directly answers his own rhetorical questions: “Why callest thou me good?” The noun (“good”) and the subject (Jesus’ goodness) match perfectly. In the CT, Jesus asks: "Why do you ask me about what is good?" and then immediately answers: “There si only One who is good.” This creates a conceptual disconnect. The young man asked about a good action to perform (“what good thing shall I do”), not WHO is good. Jesus’ follow-up- statement about the person of God being good matches the TR/MT’s personal question (“Why callest thou me good?”) far more naturally. It is rather highly probable that an early scribe, uncomfortable with the surface-level implication that Jesus was denying his own goodness or divinity, altered Matthew’s text to soften the blow, changing “Why callest thou me good?” to the more abstract: “Why do you ask me about WHAT is good?” The original reading, preserved in the TR/MT, reflects the harsher, more provocative style Jesus typically used when shattering a legalist’s paradigms.

18.x: Jesus had just told him to “keep the commandments.” The young man asks “Which?” - likely looking for a specific, high-priority command to focus on. In response, Jesus lists five of the Ten Commandments. Notice that these are all from the “second table” of the Law: the commandments that deal specifically with how we treat our fellow human beings (Ex 20:12-17).

19.x: Jesus finishes his list of specific commandments by adding a summary from Leviticus 19:18: “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” By choosing these horizontal commandments (man-to-man), Jesus is setting up a mirror for the young man to examine his true character. It is easy to claim you love God (vertical), but the proof of that love is found in how you treat the people around you: “If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 Jn 4:20 KJV).

20.x: The young man answers with total confidence, and likely complete sincerity. Externally, he had lived a moral, upright life. But his final question betrays a restless heart: “what lack I yet?” Despite his strict religious rule-following, he still feels an emptiness. He knows deep down that his morality hasn’t secured the peace or assurance of eternal life. His outward obedience had not brought him peace with God.

21.x: Jesus uses the word “perfect” here not to mean flawless sinlessness, but complete or mature. The command to sell everything was not given as a universal requirement for Christians. Jesus is exposing the very thing that this man loved more than God. The man claimed to love his neighbor as himself, but he was incredibly wealthy while others starved. Jesus isn’t teaching that we can buy our way into heaven by giving away money. He is diagnosing this specific man’s idol. The man’s wealth was his security and his ultimate love. By asking him to give it up and “follow me,” Jesus was asking, “Am I more important to you than your riches?” Notice the climax is not merely: “sell your possessions” and “give to the poor”, but: “come and follow me.” Following Christ was the issue. The wealth was standing in the way.

22.x: He walks away “sorrowful” because he realizes the cost of discipleship is higher than he is willing to pay. His “great possessions” actually possessed him. He kept the letters of the Law that were comfortable to him, but when challenged to put God above his money, he chose the money. This passage is not about rich people not being saved or that everyone must sell their possessions. This passage is about how the Law exposes our true condition before God. A person may appear morally upright yet still have an idol in his heart. Jesus demands supreme allegiance above wealth, status, or anything else. Eternal life is found in following Christ, not in trusting in our own “goodness.” The rich young man thought he had kept the commandments, but Jesus exposed how he failed the greatest one: to love God above everything else. His riches showed where his true treasure was. This sets up Jesus’ later statement that it is hard for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God (v.23-26).

The Ten Commandments are: (1) “Thou shalt have no other gods before me” (Ex 20:3 KJV) - reaffirmed in the NT in Mt 4:10; (2) “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image … Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them” (Ex 20:4-5 KJV) - reaffirmed in 1 Cor 10:14; 1 Jn 5:21; Acts 17:29; (3) “Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain” (Ex 20:7 KJV) - reaffirmed in Mt 6:9 or Jms 5:12; (4) “Remember the sabbath day” (Ex 20:8 KJV) - this is the only Commandment that is not reinstated in the NT, Jesus becomes our new rest (Col 2:16-17; Rom 14:5-6; Gal 4:9-11; Heb 4:3-11; Mk 2:27-28); (5) “Honour thy father and thy mother” (Ex 20:12 KJV) - reaffirmed in Eph 6:1-3; (6) “Thou shalt not kill(‘murder’ BSB)” (Ex 20:13 KJV) - reaffirmed in Mt 19:18; Rom 13:9 & 1 Jn 3:15, where it cites it using the Greek word for “murder”(phoneuo); (7) “Thou shalt not commit adultery” (Exo 20:14 KJV) - reaffirmed in Mt 19:18; Rom 13:9; Mt 5:27-28; (8) “Thou shalt not steal” (Exo 20:15 KJV) - reaffirmed in Mt 19:18; Rom 13:9; Eph 4:28; (9) “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16 KJV) - reaffirmed in Mt 19:18; Eph 4:25; Col 3:9; (10) “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife.. Nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s” (Exo 20:17 KJV) - reaffirmed in Rom 7:7; 13:9; Eph 5:3; Col 3:5. CATHOLICS COMBINE THE FIRST TWO COMMANDMENTS AND BREAK THE LAST ONE INTO TWO, CONCEALING THE 2ND COMMANDMENT AGAINST IMAGES AND HAVING TWO ABOUT COVETING. If you attend a Catholic class, such as pre-marriage sessions, they will hand out a list of their ten commandments: (1) I am the LORD your God: you shall not have strange Gods before me; (2) You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain; (3) Remember to keep holy the LORD’s Day; (4) Honor your father and your mother; (5) You shall not kill; (6) You shall not commit adultery; (7) You shall not steal; (8) You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor; (9) You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife; (10) You shall not covet your neighbor’s goods (CCC 2051). Notice you don’t read anything about a prohibition on either making images, nor bowing down to them nor serving them. Some of their Bibles actually add the word “gods” to Exo 20:4: “Do not bow down to those GODS(“gods” is not part of the original Hebrew), nor serve them” (Exo 20:4 Biblia Latinoamerica, the most popular Catholic Bible in countries like Mexico). Their catechism defines idolatry as: “An idolater is someone who transfers his indestructible notion of God to anything other than God.” (CCC 2114). For a Catholic to commit idolatry: “It requires man neither to believe in, nor to VENERATE, OTHER DIVINITIES than the one true God” (CCC 2112). They are not allowed to venerate any of the following: “Idolatry consists in divinizing what is not God. Man commits idolatry whenever he HONORS and REVERES A CREATURE in place of God, whether this be GODS or DEMONS (for example, satanism), POWER, PLEASURE, RACE, ANCESTORS, THE STATE, MONEY, etc.” (CCC 2113). So how can they teach all of this in their catechism and still venerate statues of Mary, Saints, and Crucifixes? Well, they also explain it in their catechism: “The divine injunction included the prohibition of every representation of God by the hand of man… Nevertheless, already in the Old Testament, God ordained or permitted the making of images that pointed symbolically toward salvation by the incarnate Word: so it was with THE BRONZE SERPENT, THE ARK OF THE COVENANT, and THE CHERUBIM. Basing itself on the mystery of THE INCARNATE WORD, the seventh ecumenical council at Nicaea (787) justified against the iconoclasts the veneration of icons — of Christ, but also of the Mother of God, the angels, and all the saints. BY BECOMING INCARNATE, THE SON OF GOD INTRODUCED A NEW ECONOMY OF IMAGES” (CCC 2129-2131). Essentially, since God became incarnate, now we can make images of God and the Saints. And “the honor rendered to an image passes to its prototype," and "whoever venerates an image venerates the person portrayed in it” & “The movement toward the image does not terminate in it as image, but tends toward that whose image it is” (CCC 2132). This, of course, is nowhere to be found in the NT, as the commandment against idols is reinforced in the NT: “flee from idolatry” (1 Cor 10:14 KJV); or “keep yourselves from idols” (1 Jn 5:21 KJV). In fact, their attempt at justifying the practice by citing the bronze serpent, the ark of the covenant and the cherubims shows their disingenuous malpractice of taking advantage of the people whom they discourage from reading by themselves: (1) The Bronze Serpent (Num 21): This actually provides the strongest biblical argument AGAINST image veneration. God commanded Moses to make a fiery serpent of brass and set it on a pole so that anyone bitten by a snake could LOOK AT IT(not venerate) and live. It was a temporary instrument of physical healing and, prophetically, a type (or shadow) or Christ being lifted up on the cross (Jn 3:14). HOWEVER, fast-forward several years, and the Israelites began treating the bronze serpent EXACTLY HOW MODERN ICONS OR STATUES ARE OFTEN TREATED: they gave it a name (Nehushtan), burned incense to it, and turned it into an object of devotional veneration. Notice how the righteous King Hezekiah reacted: "He removed the high places(altars), and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and BRAKE IN PIECES THE BRAZEN SERPENT that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan” (2 Kings 18:4 KJV). Even though the object was originally commanded by God and had a history of miraculous power, the moment it became an object of religious veneration, it was classified as idolatry and destroyed. (2) Divine Specific Command vs Human fallible initiative: Where is the source of the command for the Cherubim and the source of the command for modern statues of Mary and Saints? In the Decalogue, God issues a blanket prohibition against making graven images for religious devotion: "Thou shalt not make unto thee ANY graven image.. Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them..." (Ex 20:4-5 KJV). When the Cherubim were placed on the Ark of the Covenant, or when the bronze serpent was forged, IT WAS DONE BY DIRECT, EXPLICIT COMMAND FROM GOD TO SPECIFIC INDIVIDUALS WITH SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS (Moses and Solomon) FOR UNIQUE PURPOSES. Building an image required a specific divine exemption from the general law; and there is no scriptural command or apostolic instruction in the NT authorizing the creation or veneration of images of Mary or deceased believers. (3) No one prayed to, kissed, burned incense to, or Venerated the Objects: In the OT system, these objects were never treated as intermediaries or focal points of personal adoration. The two golden cherubim on the mercy seat (Ex 25:18-22) WERE ENTIRELY HIDDEN FROM PUBLIC VIEW. They sat within the Holy of Holies, a room entered only once a year by the High Priest alone. The common Israelite NEVER SAW THEM, LET LONE BOWED BEFORE THEM OR OFFERED PRAYERS TO THEM. They served as a physical manifestation of God’s heavenly throne room, not as individual objects of worship. Whenever the Hebrews did bow before the Ark of the Covenant, it was not directed towards the object, it was directed towards God Himself. God’s presence was localized at the Ark: Exodus 25:22 states: “there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims which are upon the ark of the testimony” (KJV). The Ark served as “the footstool of our God” (1 CH 28:2 KJV). The Ark was the place where God localized His presence among sinful people for the benefit of the covenant community. Post-Pentecost, God’s presence shifted the localized Ark to dwelling in believers through the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 3:16; 6:19). So arguing that bowing down before the Ark somehow justifies modern image veneration is disingenuous. Also, the carvings of palm trees, flowers, and cherubim inside Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:29) functioned as architectural decor to symbolize a return to the Garden of Eden: where God walked with man. They were symbols of a sacred space, not distinct holy figures meant to receive petition. These carved images were never prayed to, venerated, nor burned incense to. (4) Paul left idol makers jobless: In Acts 19:23-41, we see that Paul’s preaching about Christ directly affected the local idol-making economy. Paul was preaching in Ephesus that: “they be no gods, which are made with hands” (Acts 19:26 KJV). This message led many people to abandon idol worship, including expensive silver shrines of the goddess Diana (Artemis). A silversmith named Demetrius gathered other craftsmen and said: “Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth” (Acts 19:25 KJV). He openly admits the issue wasn’t just religion, it was money. If people stopped buying idols, then the craftsman would lose income, the temple industry would collapse, and the cult of Diana would be dishonored. So in Acts 19:26, Paul is described as attacking their religion, their livelihood, and endangering their city’s reputation and temple worship. The reaction escalated quickly: “They were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians” (Acts 19:28 KJV). A city-wide uproar breaks out and Paul is nearly killed because his preaching undermined a massive religious-business system and triggered a riot that became uncontrollable. IF CHRISTIANS HAD THEIR OWN IMAGES, THE SILVERSMITH WOULD HAPPILY MAKE MONEY SELLING THEM CHRISTIAN IDOLS, but since that wasn’t the case, Paul had to be protected. 23.x: Jesus is diagnosing the spiritual danger of wealth. Riches naturally breed self-sufficiency, pride, and a false sense of security. A person who has everything this world offers usually feels no need for a Savior. Jesus isn’t saying it is impossible for a wealthy person to be saved, but rather that their wealth creates a massive psychological and spiritual barrier to entry.

24.x: Jesus doubles down using an even stronger, more vivid illustration to drive the point home. Jesus uses Jewish hyperbole (an intentional exaggeration to make a point). BY using this imagery, Jesus is telling his disciples that, by human effort alone, it is completely impossible for someone relying on their riches to squeeze into the Kingdom of God. To be saved, a rich man must strip himself of his self-reliance, humble himself, and become spiritually bankrupt before God: something wealthy people rarely want to do. It is impossible for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. Jesus was intentionally describing something humanly impossible to set up his conclusion in v.26: “With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.”

25.x: When Jesus raises the bar of the Law so high that it seems absurd, he is deliberately driving his listeners to a point of spiritual bankruptcy. He is showing them that their own “goodness” will never be enough. Even the apostles were “exceedingly amazed,” trying to rationalize such high standards set by Jesus. In first-century Jewish culture, wealth was viewed as a direct sign of God’s blessing and righteousness (Deut 28). The common logic was: “If anyone is going to heaven, it’s the rich guy who can afford to give alms, buy the best sacrifices, and spend his time studying Torah.” The disciples’ question it in despair: “Who then can be saved?” They realize that if the best-behaved, most blessed, law-abiding rich man cannot squeeze through the eye of the needle, then the average fisherman, tax collector, or sinner stands absolutely zero chance.

26.x: “With men this is impossible”: Jesus does not soften the blow. He doesn’t say: “Well, it’s just really, really hard.” He agrees with their despair. By human strength, human mortality, human rule-following, and human devotion, salvation is an absolute, flat-out impossibility. “But with God all things are possible”: This is the bridge of the gospel. What man cannot do for himself, God must do for him. Salvation cannot be earned; it must be given as a supernatural act of God. The disciples struggled to understand this because, like most people, they were conditioned to believe that religion is a ladder you climb. They thought Jesus was just a new Rabbi giving them better instructions on how to climb. Throughout the gospels, Jesus systematically smashes that ladder. In the Sermon of the Mount, he tells them their righteousness must EXCEED that of the scribes and Pharisees (Mt 5:20) - the absolute Olympic gold-medalists of rule-following. He then commands: “Be ye therefore PERFECT, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect” (Mt 5:48 KJV). And then he tells the morally “flawless” young, rich ruler to sell literally everything he owns. Jesus wasn’t giving a checklist for entering heaven: he was using the Law as a mirror to show them their inability to keep it. As the apostle would later explain in Galatians 3:24: “the law was our schoolmaster(‘tutor’ WEB) to bring us unto Christ.” By demanding absolute perfection, Jesus forces us to our knees to say: “I can’t do this.” And that is exactly where salvation begins. The moment we admit it is humanly impossible, we stop relying on our resume and start relying entirely on Jesus’ finished work on the cross, where his perfect righteousness is credited to us as a free gift: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mt 18:3 KJV) - only by becoming a child that depends 100% on his Father for salvation do we achieve salvation.

27.x: True to his personality, Peter speaks out to try to process this out loud, trying to figure out where he and the other disciples stand. “Behold, we have forsaken all”: They DID do what the rich young ruler refused to do: they left everything to follow Jesus. Peter is looking for reassurance. The young ruler wouldn’t give up his wealth, but Peter, Andrew, James, and John had literally walked away from their fishing businesses, boats, nets, and families the moment Jesus called them. “What shall we have therefore?”: It’s a very raw, human question. Peter is essentially asking: “Since salvation is impossible by human effort, and we’ve risked absolutely everything to rely entirely on you, what is our outcome? Was it worth it?”

28.x: “In the regeneration”: The Greek word here (palingenesia) means a “new birth,” “renewal,” or “restoration.” Jesus is pointing them to the future cosmic renewal, the creation of the New Heavens and the New Earth when God fixes everything broken by sin. Jesus doesn’t rebuke Peter for asking. Instead, he promises the twelve apostles a staggering place of honor and authority in his future kingdom. Because they stood by him during his rejection on earth, they will reign with him in his glory. Notice it’s always 12: rule with Christ on 12 thrones (v.28), the foundation built on all the 12 apostles (Eph 2:20), and the New Jerusalem built on 12 foundations, one for each apostle (Rev 21:14). Peter had the same authority as the rest of the apostles. He was never singled out to have a singled-out primacy over the others.

29.x: “And every one”: Jesus immediately expands the promise beyond just the twelve apostles to every single believer across history. Following Jesus always costs something. Sometimes it costs relationships, reputation, or material security. But Jesus promises that whatever you lose for his sake, God replaces “an hundrefold.” He isn’t promising a literal hundred houses, but rather that the spiritual family, community, peace, and joy you gain in Christ infinitely outweigh whatever you walk away from. “And shall inherit”: Notice the word “inherit.” YOU DON’T EARN AN INHERITANCE BY WORKING; you receive it simply by being a child of the Father. Salvation is a gift of God’s grace, not of works so that no one may boast (Eph 2:8-9).

30.x: Jesus is warning Peter and the disciples against pride. Yes, they left everything first, but they must not look down on others. In the world’s eyes, the rich young ruler was “first” (sucessful, righteous, blessed) and the disciples were “last” (poor fishermen). But in God’s Kingdom, the rich man walked away with nothing, and the bankrupt fishermen inherited everything. God values broken, humble dependence over self-righteous status. This exact verse (v.30) is actually the setup for the next chapter. To explain what he means by “the last shall be first,” Jesus immediately launches into the parable of the Laborere in the Vineyard (Mt 20), where workers who only labored for one hour get paid the exact same wage as those who slaved all day, showing that Kingdom rewards are driven by God’s astonishing grace, not our seniority or merit. And, while the immediate context addresses the disciples’ attitudes toward rewards and humility, the principle of “the first shall be last; and the last shall be first” has a historical and prophetic application to the Jews and the Gentiles (us, non-Jews): (1) Israel was “First” in God’s timeline: historically and covenantally, the Jewish people were unquestionably “first.” Even when Jesus came, he’d say to the disciples: "Go not into the way of the Gentiles... But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (Mt 10:5-6 KJV). They had the front-row seat to the Messiah. By all accounts, they should have been the first to enter the kingdom. (2) The Great Inversion: Matthew 21 & 22: Jesus gives the parable of the Wicked Husbandmen (Mt 21:33-43). The religious leaders (Jews) reject and kill the householder’s son (Jesus). Jesus looks directly at them and says: “Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof" (v. 43). He also gives the parable of the Wedding Feast (Mt 22:1-10), where the bidden guests (Israel) refuse to come to the wedding king’s feast and even kill his servants. The king then says the guests “were not worthy” and sends his servants into the highways to gather “as many as they should find”: both bad and good (the Gentiles). (3) In Luke’s account, Jesus explicitly says so: "And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south [the Gentiles], and shall sit down in the kingdom of God. So while the Gentiles are currently enjoying the "first" position of blessing in the Church age because the Jews rejected Christ, God's ultimate plan is that this very blessing will eventually turn the hearts of the Jewish people back to their Messiah (although through suffering and persecution: Rev 12:6,13-17), proving once again that the Kingdom operates entirely on unexpected, unmerited grace.
